title: Dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested over air base security incident
summary: The 27-year-old man was arrested in London, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said.
story: Police on Thursday arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at the U.S.-run RAF Fairford air base in England that British authorities have linked to Tehran.
The 27-year-old man was arrested in London on Thursday, and police have searched two properties in the U.K. capital, Counter Terrorism Policing said in a statement.
A 26-year-old British national was interviewed by police "under caution," which means the interview was recorded and can be used in future prosecutions.

On Sunday, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. The suspects have since been released on bail.
Their quick release drew criticism from President Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But it also prompted questions in the U.K. as to whether the authorities had overreacted.
Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the investigation "is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry."
"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles - including possible foreign state involvement," she said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. sees "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. Iran denies involvement.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
The base 100 miles west of London has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year's war with Iran.

Iranian authorities have warned that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets, but the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement shared Monday on social media that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Burnham said authorities have the investigation under "the strongest grip and the closest control," and British officials had been "talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done."

U.K. officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

title: Ditch the dating app. Meet an Irish town's 83-year-old mystical matchmaker.
summary: Want to find love the old-fashioned way? You might consider a date with Willie Daly, the legendary third-generation matchmaker of Lisdoonvarna.
story: Lisdoonvarna, Ireland — For nearly two centuries, a small Irish town has lured singletons to a festival every September that sees hopeful romantics seek their one true love.

The monthlong matchmaking festival that started in 1857 has become a global event, attracting over 60,000 visitors annually to the rugged landscape of County Clare, and specifically to the tiny town of Lisdoonvarna.
The festival even broke into American pop culture, featuring several years ago on the sitcom "Schitt's Creek."

In many ways, it's an old-world solution to modern dating. There is no app and no algorithms, just a chance to meet a match organically, through Irish traditional dancing and music, speed dating — or through the matchmaking skills of 83-year-old local legend Willie Daly.

Daly's grandfather helped start the festival, and his family has been pairing couples for three generations. In his father's and grandfather's day, many Irish towns and villages had traditional matchmakers, but Daly is now believed to be among the last, if not the last, keeping the tradition alive.

If prospective suitors wish to find a match through Daly, they meet with him and fill out a form outlining their hobbies, personality traits, and what they're looking for in a partner. Through his somewhat mystical personal intuition, Daly will then find a match and send the pair off on a first date.

"When I'm walking down the street, often I'd meet people … two or three couples said, 'You fixed us up 30 years ago, or 40 years ago,'" Daly told CBS News last month. "We're lucky here. Now this is a wonderful festival, and it's a great provision of opportunity — the opportunity to get married is very consistent in it. Music and dancing all day long, you know, for 30 days."
In a tattered old book, Daly keeps records of the hopeful matches he's arranged over the years, and local legend has it that if you place two hands on the book, you'll be married within six months.

Daly's image is literally etched on the front of a local watering hole — The Matchmaker Bar, where singles gather every year to drink, dance and try to meet their future spouse — in a testament to his stature in Lisdoonvarna.
CBS News attended the festivities at the pub in September and spoke with young attendees about what they were looking for in an ideal partner.
"I suppose a bit of loyalty, a bit of values, but also a bit of craic, you can't beat a bit of craic," said one young woman, using a common Irish phrase that translates roughly to good fun.
"Someone agricultural. I am agricultural myself … we're farming at home, we have a sheep farm at home. That's what I'm looking for at the moment," an Irishman said about his hunt for love.
Another attendee, Erica, told CBS News she had traveled all the way from Colombia for the festival.

"It's the opportunity to meet people the right way, face-to-face," she said. "Those apps, I mean, I'm not saying that people are hiding anything, but right now, just having the contact, just to sit there and talk to people makes [dating] a whole different event."
American Mary Timby from Colorado came to the village last year and ended up going viral, garnering over 2 million views after posting online about how she found love at the matchmaking festival.
She returned this year, and is now an ambassador for the event.

"I first heard about the festival on 'Schitt's Creek.' It was during COVID. I was huddled in a blanket on my couch and I Googled it and I thought, 'Oh, it's a real festival. Wouldn't it be fun if I just went someday?'" she said.

"My partner is from Ennis, here in County Clare, and we met at The Matchmaking Bar," she said. "I loved the Irish accent, and he just, was funny. He made me laugh and we connected right away, so we exchanged information."
But Timby's story shows that even matchmaking with nearly 170 years of proven success can benefit from modern technology.
"He found me on social media the next day," she said of her match. "And the rest is history."

title: Bolivia's attorney general arrested for alleged money laundering, drug trafficking
summary: The U.S. State Department said that Roger Mariaca received "bribes to facilitate drug trafficking and help violent criminals evade justice."
story: Bolivia's attorney general arrested for alleged money laundering and drug trafficking

U.S.-sanctioned Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca has been arrested on suspicion of money laundering and drug trafficking, with police finding bundles of cash smuggled out of his house, the government said Thursday.
Mariaca was arrested on Wednesday night in the eastern city of Santa Cruz, two days after the United States revoked his visa due to his alleged links to drug trafficking.
"A criminal organization entrenched in the justice system has been dismantled," Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo told a press conference.
Oviedo said that in the early hours of Thursday, four people were caught trying to remove bundles of cash from Mariaca's house aboard an ambulance.
A video released by the interior ministry showed police removing wads of cash from the ambulance's panels.
Oviedo said that the Attorney General's Office, "headed by Roger Mariaca, became a criminal organization dedicated to protecting, encouraging, and safeguarding narco-terrorism."

According to the Reuters news agency, a prosecutor's office official reported the "abduction" of Mariaca during a live broadcast. Local media said Mariaca had been detained at Viru Viru International Airport, Reuters reported.
The U.S. State Department said Monday that Mariaca received "bribes to facilitate drug trafficking and help violent criminals evade justice." Mariaca has denied the allegations.
Oviedo said that Mariaca's arrest took place with the "cooperation of the U.S. government" as part of the "fight against terrorism."
In total, four prosecutors, six employees of the public prosecutor's office and the four people found aboard the ambulance were arrested.

The raids come as Bolivia's center-right President Rodrigo Paz, who took office in November 2025, seeks to strengthen ties with the United States after two decades of socialist rule marked by mutual enmity.
On Monday, the U.S. revoked the visas of 12 Bolivian officials and nine other Bolivian nationals who do not currently have visas were rendered ineligible to receive them.
In March, Paz took Bolivia into the "Shield of the Americas," a U.S.-led alliance of right-wing Latin American governments to combat transnational organized crime.
"Mariaca is my friend"
Mariaca was appointed attorney general in October 2024.

The Attorney General's Office stated in a press release that, given Mariaca's "definitive absence," the next most senior public prosecutor, Luis Montano Morales, would replace him on an interim basis.
Mariaca's lawyer Romel Ipamo told local media that his client would "cooperate fully" with the investigation.

During Mariaca's tenure, Bolivian police captured Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastian Marset earlier this year. Marset, who was on the U.S.' most-wanted fugitives list, was passed to agents of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at the Santa Cruz airport, then put on a U.S. airplane, state TV showed. In March, he made his first appearance in a federal court in Virginia.
Local media on Wednesday broadcast a video purporting to show Marset on the day of his arrest declaring: "Mariaca is my friend."
AFP has been unable to verify the authenticity of the video.
Police also raided the headquarters of the public prosecutor's office in the southern city of Sucre, according to footage shared by the police on social media.
Surrounded by hooded police officers, Claudia Pardo, head of communications for the prosecutor's office, denounced the raid as "illegal."
She told AFP later that she was under arrest.
The public prosecutor's offices in Santa Cruz and La Paz were also targeted in the nationwide raids, according to images broadcast by local media.

title: Co-pilot stabs captain, tries to crash FlyDubai flight en route to Israel
summary: Israel leader Benjamin Netanyahu says the FlyDubai co-pilot who allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to crash the plane had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination."
story: A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after a violent attempt by the co-pilot to seize control of the aircraft and crash it, passengers and Israeli officials said.

"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers and other crew members who intervened. The prime minister said he instructed Israel's "security establishment to prepare for potential additional threats."
Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning.

An Israeli security official told CBS News authorities were investigating the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack, which was thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit, overpowered the terrorist, and with their own hands returned control of the aircraft to an additional flight crew that was present," according to a statement.
However, in an interview with CBS News later Wednesday, Netanyahu indicated that the co-pilot's motive was still unknown.

"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said, referencing witness accounts. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."

The plane diverted to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base. No passengers were injured in the incident, but the pilot who was attacked by his fellow crew member reportedly sustained stab wounds, and Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
Passenger Asaf Rajuan has been credited with fighting off the attacker in the cockpit before two off-duty pilots took control of the plane.

"Whoever is hearing me, we need help," Rajuan said in a video posted to social media from the plane after the co-pilot had been subdued. "We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don't know. All the passengers are OK, but not the pilot. We need help."

According to Netanyahu, the pilot who carried out the stabbing was placed under arrest and was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities." An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

In a social media post, the Israel Foreign Ministry identified the wounded pilot as Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian national. It described him as a "hero" who "fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit."
According to the foreign ministry, Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door to allow passengers and crew to enter and intervene.
"Together, their extraordinary courage saved 174 lives," the foreign ministry said.

In a brief statement posted online Thursday, India's Ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal said he was "very reassured" after meeting Machchhar. The Indian embassy said in a separate post that the pilot was "in good health and recovering well."

The plane landed in Tel Aviv shortly before 8 p.m. local time on Wednesday. People could be heard singing and chanting as the passengers disembarked. Family members came to the airport to celebrate their loved ones' safe return.

One passenger said the plane dropped "very, very sharply suddenly" multiple times before balancing out. Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place over Jordan.

"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."

"There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," Ohayon said.

Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
One passenger seated at the front of the plane said a "group of young people fought" with the attacker.

The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information. CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.

The Israeli Air Force was first to notice something was wrong, an Israeli official with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News. The air force noticed the flight deviating from its flight path and descending at an alarming rate, the official said. When it tried to contact the plane, it received no response. It then got the emergency alert that specified a hijacking, not just a distress call.

At that point, according to the official, the flight was still several hundred miles from Israeli airspace. However, even 90 seconds or so into the incident, the air force feared a 9/11-style attack, so it immediately made the decision to close Israeli airspace, and seconds after that it scrambled several jets, the official said.
The jets never left Israeli airspace because it became clear that the plane had turned toward Saudi Arabia, and that Saudi Arabia had scrambled its own jets, the official said.
This sequence of events occurred within the span of about two to three minutes, according to the official, and the entire episode lasted about 15 minutes.

A statement from FlyDubai said only that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and that the aircraft "was successfully secured by on-duty FlyDubai crew traveling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely" in Saudi Arabia.

The airline said "all passengers and crew are safe and accounted for," and it confirmed that two replacement aircraft had been deployed to Tabuk to "relieve the passengers and crew," though many Israeli passengers told media outlets they would not reboard a FlyDubai plane.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," the airline said in its statement, urging "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that there were four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship aboard the flight.

Netanyahu had warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.
Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.

Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."

Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in the upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X: "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."
"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday, saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."
"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

title: Pakistani airstrikes kill 10 civilians in Afghanistan, U.N. mission says
summary: Pakistan says airstrikes in Afghanistan killed 22 terrorists, but Afghanistan's Taliban regime and the U.N. mission in the country say mostly children were killed.
story: Islamabad — Pakistan launched new airstrikes in Afghanistan overnight, killing at least 10 people, most of them children, the United Nations mission in the country said Thursday.

Islamabad claimed the attacks targeted militants with Pakistani insurgent groups who have mounted attacks on the country, but Afghanistan's Taliban government accused the neighboring nation of aggression, saying the strikes hit civilian homes, killing women and children.

"UNAMA has confirmed that at least 10 civilians were killed, most of them children, and 9 people injured in airstrikes," the United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in a statement shared on social media. UNAMA did not attribute the strikes to Pakistan, but no other nation has claimed recent aerial attacks on Afghanistan.
The strikes targeted areas in Afghanistan's Kunar and Helmand provinces, and chief spokesperson for the Afghan regime Zabihullah Mujahid said three civilian homes were destroyed.
He condemned the Pakistani bombing as an act of aggression.
Pakistan's Ministry of Information presented a sharply different account.

In a statement sent to CBS News, the ministry said the strikes were intelligence-driven, "well planned and calibrated" and hit militant hideouts and camps at two locations, and that "initial reports suggest the killing of 22 terrorists."
The ministry claimed "large quantities of weapons and ammunition" were also destroyed in the strikes.
"The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan," Pakistan's information ministry said. "Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs."

"Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs," it said, adding that its attacks would "continue at full pace to wipe out" alleged terror groups operating in Afghanistan.
Videos circulating from the scene of strikes in Helmand province, near the Pakistan border, showed people searching through the rubble of a destroyed mud-wall house, finding remains.
Ebad Khan, a resident in Kunar province, told CBS News one of the strikes hit a home belonging to a family that had moved in only a day earlier.
"They had children and livestock. They had just moved from another district," he said. "Unfortunately, all six members of the family were killed, including children."

Repeated cross-border clashes between the neighbors have escalated this year, with Pakistan carrying out airstrikes inside Afghanistan on multiple occasions. The countries have long accused each other of allowing terrorist groups to operate along their shared border, plotting attacks on civilians and security forces.
According to UNAMA, the clashes have caused more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries in Afghanistan this year alone.

title: U.S. surrogate for Chinese billionaire says she trusted agency, as questions arise
summary: The CEO of the surrogacy agency Patriot Conceptions says he was unaware billionaire Xu Bo was building a massive family.
story: A surrogate carrying a child for Chinese billionaire Xu Bo — a man reported to have over 100 children — said she trusted her agency to "protect surrogates." Now, the business practices of California-based Patriot Conceptions and its CEO are facing fresh scrutiny.

Stanford University's Hoover Institution, where the company's CEO Haotian Bai formerly served as a fellow, cut ties with him last week, shortly after a CBS Sunday Morning investigation featuring the surrogate put a spotlight on loopholes and accusations of questionable practices in the commercial surrogacy industry. A subsequent story in the New York Post looked at Bai's background.

"He is no longer affiliated with the Hoover Institution," the institution said on its website. "In light of recent media reports, it is clear that Mr. Bai misled the Institution on the nature of his businesses."
During his 2024-25 fellowship, Bai focused on veterans' access to in vitro fertilization. He frequently advertises his surrogacy agency as veteran-founded.
Bai said in a 2019 court declaration, filed in a dispute with a former business partner, that he served in the U.S. Army in Afghanistan until 2017 and that he'd been diagnosed with PTSD.

A U.S. Army spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that Bai served as a chemical operations specialist from November 2013 to October 2017. However, the Army said that while he assisted with units that were preparing to deploy, he never deployed himself.
"He had no deployments and left the Army in the rank of specialist," said Christopher Surridge, a U.S. Army spokesperson.

After leaving the military, Bai co-founded another surrogacy agency in 2018. He ended up in a court battle with his co-founder a year later. The case was later voluntarily dismissed. Bai founded Patriot Conceptions in 2019

The Hoover Institution said it would conduct "a full internal review" of the application process for the Veteran Fellowship Program. CBS News reached out to Patriot Conceptions, and in a written response, Bai said he went through "a normal application process as a U.S. Army veteran for a Hoover Institution fellowship in 2023 and was selected through what appeared to be their usual channels and protocols to be a fellow." The statement said there was "no point at which Mr Bai 'misled' the Hoover Institution about his research or his intentions."
Bai's surrogacy agency caters to international clients, who make up 40% of its business — with an emphasis on intended parents from China.
The U.S. is the only developed country where commercial surrogacy is widely legal, attracting foreign nationals who don't have the option in their country, with a large percentage coming from China.

It remains unclear how Patriot Conceptions initially agreed to provide a surrogate for Xu Bo, a video game executive who is well known in China. Patriot Conceptions partnered with a global surrogacy agency representing the intended father.

The surrogate, whom CBS News is calling Judy to protect her identity, said she first learned who the intended parent was on the night before her embryo transfer in April, after traveling from her home state to California for the procedure.
Documents obtained by CBS News showed that the intended father was Xu, who has boasted online about his desire to father large numbers of children.

A single mother, Judy said she decided to become a surrogate because she wanted to use the payment to create a better life for herself and her daughter. She said she also liked the idea of helping someone build a family — but added that she never imagined it would be that large.
"You don't think to ask … 'Oh, do they have, like, over 100 babies already?'" she said in an interview.

In an earlier phone conversation with CBS News, Bai asked whether Judy's surrogacy records had been offered for sale on the dark web. CBS News obtained the records from whistleblowers concerned about irregularities in the surrogacy industry.
During the call, Bai dismissed media reports detailing the scale of Xu's family.

Xu, a reclusive billionaire who is rarely seen in public, made his fortune as founder of Guangzhou Duoyi Network, one of China's largest mobile game companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the number of children Xu is said to have fathered via surrogacy, as well as other Chinese billionaires building mega-families.

His company said in a December statement that Xu had 12 children born in the U.S. via surrogates, but acknowledged a larger overall total: "Regarding the rumors about the number of children … the actual number is only a little over one hundred."

Six months later, Xu posted a photo of young children seated in rows alongside a statement: "Mr. Xu Bo believes in the philosophy that more children bring more blessings, and he wishes for all his words and actions to benefit the long-term development of the Chinese nation."
CBS News reached out to Xu directly and through representatives but received no response.

Addressing media coverage in a recent statement, Xu wrote: "Overseas media outlets have previously produced numerous misinterpretations and unfriendly reports about China, as a Chinese citizen safeguarding China's interests, Xu stands on the same side as the Chinese government and avoids granting interviews to overseas media unless necessary."

Following the publication of the CBS News report on Sept. 13, Patriot Conceptions said the firm's employees had encouraged Judy to terminate her contract after public reports about the size of Xu's family surfaced in December.
A statement issued by Patriot Conceptions stated that "it did not know the wider scale of Xu's family described in later public reporting." Patriot Conceptions declined to be interviewed on camera.

Judy disputed this account, stating that the agency "never" advised her to terminate the agreement. She said agency representatives visited her hotel room following her embryo transfer in April to bring her "flowers and snacks."
Judy said the agency told her after she matched that the intended parent was a "single father looking to expand their family."
"I felt like I trusted this agency to kind of protect surrogates and match them with people with good intentions," Judy said.
Judy said when the agency mentioned a large family, she was picturing something from a movie.
"'[The] Sound of Music.' Do you know that movie? My immediate first thought, 'Oh, that would be really cute,' like a family of 10 kids," she said.

title: Netanyahu says it's too early to determine motive in cockpit stabbing
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News that the motive of the Flydubai co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv is still unknown.
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News on Wednesday that the motive of the co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a passenger jet bound from Dubai to Tel Aviv was still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.

"I think it looks like a suicide attempt simply because of what this hero Yaniv described when he went in," Netanyahu speculated, referring to Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers on the FlyDubai flight who has been credited with entering the cockpit and helping to subdue the attacker.

"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said of the co-pilot, whose identity has not been revealed. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."

Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
According to Israeli officials, on Wednesday morning local time, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot stabbed the captain.
Per data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News, the plane then plunged about 17,000 feet, climbed 5,000 feet, and then fell another 7,000 feet before stabilizing.

Israeli officials and passengers said the captain, an Indian national, was able to fight off his co-pilot and unlock the cockpit door. Witnesses recounted how a group of passengers and crew members then stormed the cockpit and subdued the co-pilot.

Two off-duty pilots then took control of the plane and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. There were 174 people on board, Israeli officials said. Most of the passengers later boarded a replacement FlyDubai plane and were flown to Ben Gurion International Airport, arriving Wednesday night.

An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker, whose name has not been released, was born in Oman and holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Netanyahu told CBS News he was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia.
"He'll be, I assume, moved very quickly to Dubai," Netanyahu told CBS News, adding that Israeli authorities will "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."

A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the pilot to the UAE for questioning.
Asked if he thought the incident could have stemmed from a mental health issue and not an act of terrorism, Netanyahu said, "it could be, I don't know, we'll find out soon."

"We've had signs that Iran, and particularly through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad," Netanyahu added. "But I think it's too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."

No definitive motive for the stabbing has been determined by authorities. An Israeli security official previously told CBS News that investigators were looking into the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," FlyDubai said in its own statement. It urged "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."

title: Passengers recount terrifying attempted hijack of Dubai-to-Israel flight
summary: Passenger Ron Levi tells CBS News the attempted hijack of a Dubai-to-Israel flight was "the scariest thing possible."
story: Passenger accounts paint a chaotic and terrifying picture of the alleged attempted hijacking of FlyDubai Flight 1073 on Wednesday. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed his counterpart and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft.

"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers he said had helped to "neutralize the pilot."
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack."
"It was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives," passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday.
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship were aboard the flight.
Here's what we know about how the suspected terror attack unfolded, based on accounts from Levi and other passengers.
"Worse than a free-fall"

"The flight was going well, we were two hours in," Levi told CBS News' Dov Lieber, speaking from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where the plane made its safe emergency landing, piloted by an off-duty flight crew member who happened to be on board.
"All of a sudden, what we thought was turbulence started," said Levi. It kept getting stronger, and "we realized it's not something regular."
"I would say much worse than a free-fall," he said, describing how the plane "started turning all sideways and going up and down in all different kinds of directions, for a pretty long time."
"It's very hard to even to estimate if this was 30 seconds or a minute or more than that … it was just the scariest thing possible."
Levi was sitting in a row of seats with his family, "just holding each other's hands and saying that we love them and just hoping for the best."
"And then shouting started from the front of the plane," he recalled. He saw some people near the front get up.
"Very stressful situation"

Passenger Adam Polo was in row 13, hugging his 6-year-old son while his wife was hugging their 3-year-old daughter. Polo told CBS News he "tried to be cool" for his children and told them, "We will be OK."

"The first couple of minutes was very terrifying; you just feel like you're going to crash, but even after the plane was stabilizing, there was more than an hour where we were in the air without the primary crew members," Polo said.
Polo said he couldn't see much from his seat, but after 15 minutes, he saw a passenger running out of the cockpit covered in blood.
"No one from the crew members told us what was happening," Polo said. "The only ones to give us information was the passengers who stood up with an act of bravery."
Polo, who lives in Israel and was vacationing in Thailand with his family, said everything happened so fast and it was a "very stressful situation."
"I'm a pretty cynical guy, I'm not getting excited easily, but I think it was one of the most exciting moments of my life when the plane touched the ground," Polo said.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot"

Levi said he wasn't close enough to see what happened next, but several other passengers who spoke with Israeli media said one pilot had stabbed the other, details that were also repeated by Netanyahu.
"According to the initial information in our possession, the terrorist's intention was one thing: to crash the plane with all its passengers," said Katz, Israel's defense chief.

Netanyahu said he had spoken with an Israeli passenger who told him that, "somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit together with one of the crew members, and that together they neutralized the pilot who carried out the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems."
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place, she believed somewhere over Jordan.

"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone, held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."

Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
Netanyahu said the person who "managed to stabilize the aircraft" was "another aircrew member who was on the plane."

"All we heard in the back was shouting," said Levi. "We saw that some people were dealing with stuff, and it kept on going like that for, I think, about 10, 20 minutes until … the shakiness [of the plane] relaxed."
"Rumors started coming, and we realized that it wasn't just turbulence," he said. "It was something … a lot worse than that."
"They're heroes," he said of the people who intervened to stop the attacking pilot. "We owe them our lives."
Levi said he saw people covered in blood.
"They're here with us as well now," he told CBS News from the airport in Saudi Arabia. "These were the people I'm talking about who … jumped into the cockpit even and saved the situation."
According to Ohayon, a doctor and others on board helped treat the pilot for unspecified wounds.
"Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," she said.
"I just want to go home"
An Israeli security official told CBS News on Wednesday that Israel is investigating whether it was intended to be a Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
The pilot was arrested and taken for questioning by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was working to bring the passengers back to Israel safely.
"There's another FlyDubai plane here now," said Levi. "People are a bit reluctant to get on it, naturally. … We want to go home, but we want to do it in a safe way."
Asked how he was processing the incident, Levi replied: "Honestly, I'm not even starting. We're all shaking here … I have no idea. I just want to go home."
The flight landed safely in Tel Aviv around 8 p.m. local time Wednesday. Cheers and chants could be heard as the passengers disembarked.

summary: Johnny Depp's transformation as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer sparked debate over its "think again" tagline and revisionist marketing.

The actor’s turn as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer released Thursday earned enthusiastic praise from fans, while the film’s suggestion that audiences should "think again" about the classic story left others scratching their heads.

title: Gordon Ramsay admits real reason he was crying while walking daughter down the aisle
summary: Gordon Ramsay reveals feeling "second best" after walking Holly Ramsay down the aisle and jokes about what really made him cry at the wedding.
story: "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars" executive producer Gordon Ramsay opens up about why he really became emotional while giving away his daughter Holly at her wedding.
Gordon Ramsay opened up about the bittersweet experience of giving away his daughter, Holly Ramsay, at her wedding.

Holly, 26, married Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty, 31, in December 2025 after the couple announced their engagement in 2024. The 59-year-old celebrity chef shares Holly, her twin brother Jack, daughters Megan, 28, and Matilda, 24, and sons Oscar, 7, and Jesse, 2, with his wife, Tana Ramsay, 52, whom he married in 1996.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Ramsay, who is starring in season two of Apple TV's "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars," reflected on the close bonds that he shares with his three daughters and explained why he was left feeling "second best" after he walked Holly down the aisle.
GORDON RAMSAY SAYS ‘THE MOST IMPORTANT THING’ HE TAUGHT HIS SIX KIDS HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH COOKING

Gordon Ramsay revealed the real reason that he was crying while walking his daughter Holly down the aisle during her wedding last year. (Grant Buchanan/Dave Benett/Getty Images; Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images)

"You grow up with these gorgeous girls and you teach them. I said to them, from an early age, they must have been 7 or 8 years of age, ‘The earlier you tell me, the more I can f---ing do," he recalled.

"They ignore you for two or three years," Ramsay continued. "But when they get to 11 or 12, ‘Hey daddy, you know what he said to me? The earlier you told me, the more you can do, I have a problem. Can I talk to you about it?’"
KELLY RIPA, MARK CONSUELOS SHARE BLUNT ADVICE FOR COUPLES PLANNING A BIG WEDDING

"Bang, then we're in,'" he added with a smile. "Then you're like that, you're sort of the BFF, right? Then you're a cool f---ing dad, then you're perfect. But when you walk them down the aisle, and you're minutes away from not being the number one guy in their life, and you're handing them over, man, that hits. That absolutely hits."
"So you have to understand that that relationship with your daughter is borrowed time before there's another man in their lives. Another partner in their life, that you become second best."
WATCH: GORDON RAMSAY ADMITS REAL REASON HE WAS CRYING WHILE WALKING DAUGHTER DOWN THE AISLE
The "Hell's Kitchen" star noted that as a father of six, he will have to experience those moments multiple times in the future.
"I have ages to go through all that s---," he said. "Three boys and three girls."
Ramsay is pictured with his daughters Holly Ramsay Peaty and Tilly Ramsay in May 2026. (Grant Buchanan/Dave Benett/Getty Images)
Ramsay, who is famous for his fiery temper and tough demeanor in the kitchen, admitted to becoming emotional at Holly's wedding but joked that it was not for the reason that most people would expect.

"I was like a sack of f---ing custard walking down that bloody — that line — into that church. 60 meters!" he recalled. "And I was looking at all these flowers overlooking the pews and thinking, ‘S---, this is expensive!' Everyone thought I was crying because I was giving her away. I was more crying with the f---ing cost of the flower bill, and where are they going tomorrow? We're paying all this money for 90 minutes, these flowers."
DANA PERINO: FIVE IMPORTANT LESSONS FROM MY FATHER FOR EVERY PROUD GIRL DAD
Ramsay quipped that his tears dried up once he realized that the flowers could be repurposed for a good cause.
"We got the flowers donated to the local hospital and that stopped me crying," he said. "And then I handed her over, and I celebrated like no tomorrow, because that daughter was expensive."
Ramsay's oldest daughter Megan is engaged. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)
CLINT BLACK AND LISA HARTMAN BLACK'S ONE RULE THAT HAS KEPT THEIR MARRIAGE STRONG FOR NEARLY 35 YEARS

Holly and Peaty's wedding took place on Dec. 27, 2025, at The Abbey Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul in Bath, England. During a January interview with People, Ramsay admitted that he was nervous about giving his father-of-the-bride speech.

"It's tough, honestly — I mean, being a dad with three daughters, you dream of that moment. That moment arrives, and you're just like a hot mess," he told the outlet. "The speech was perfect. It went well. You got to find that sort of — you've got to be warm, emotional ... It was just a tough gig."
Tilly told People that Ramsay spent about an hour rehearsing his speech in front of her on Christmas Eve. She said that while Ramsay pored over every word, ultimately "no tweaks were needed."
"It was perfect," Tilly said. "It made everybody cry."
Ramsay said that he was crying due to the hefty price tag of the wedding flowers. (PA Images via Getty Images)
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY

Holly wore three different dresses on her wedding day, including her mother's gown from her 1996 nuptials with Ramsay. The TV personality told People that seeing Holly in Tana's wedding dress came as "a bit of a shock."

While speaking with British Vogue in January, Holly noted that wearing the gown during her father-daughter dance with Ramsay was especially meaningful because "the last time Dad saw this dress was when he danced with my mom at their wedding."
At the time, Holly told the outlet that Ramsay became emotional whenever she discussed the wedding leading up to her big day.
Holly married Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty on Dec. 27, 2025. (PA Images via Getty Images)
"Dad cries every time I talk about the wedding," she said. "The other day I was asking him which car he and I would take to the church, and he welled up immediately."

Though Holly is the first of Ramsay's six children to walk down the aisle, he will soon have to give another daughter away. In an August appearance on "Live with Kelly and Mark," he revealed that Megan was engaged.
During his interview with Fox News Digital, Ramsay noted that he needed to start preparing for Megan's nuptials.
"I've got to get my dance act together, especially with another wedding coming up next year," he said.
Ramsay said giving Holly away made him feel "second best." (WireImage)

"Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars," which is executive produced by Ramsay, made its debut on Apple TV in October 2025. Hosted by food expert Jesse Burgess, the documentary series follows chefs around the world as they pursue Michelin stars while balancing the personal and professional sacrifices required to achieve culinary excellence.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Ramsay admitted that his own pursuit of perfection in the kitchen had come at a cost. Looking back, the "MasterChef" star reflected on the biggest sacrifice that he made while building his restaurant empire.
"Time," he said. "You become one of the most, sort of, you know, selfish individuals because you need to focus. And so I'd say the sacrifice was less time with the family straight off the bat."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Ramsay and his wife Tana share six children. (Gordon Ramsay Instagram)

"There's a lot of situations in ‘Knife Edge,' you'll see families working together. That's actually harder," he continued. "My wife and I decided that 'Look, the time we have is little, but it'd be quality.' It won't be great, long time, but it would be quality. And then my kids appreciate the time they had with me."

"They didn't see me seven nights a week," Ramsay said. "I didn't do the school runs. I wasn't doing the dinners and the goodbyes and the plays and all the nativities. I couldn't do that. And so, don't forget when all your mates are out celebrating, you're working because they're either eating at the restaurants or out going to another restaurant."
"So yeah, I'd say time, the biggest, the most expensive ingredient in the world, time," he added. "And you have to sacrifice that time."

Ramsay, whose restaurants currently hold nine Michelin stars worldwide, has earned a total of 17 Michelin stars over the course of his career. His flagship Restaurant Gordon Ramsay in London has held the maximum three Michelin stars continuously since 2001. Ramsay's portfolio gained a ninth star earlier this year when Restaurant Gordon Ramsay High in London's Bishopsgate area earned its first Michelin star in the 2026 Michelin Guide.

The second season of "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars" premiered on Sept. 25. (Apple TV)

According to the official synopsis, season two of "Knife Edge" "follows 16 restaurants at pivotal moments in their journeys: A chef and his family risk everything to put a tiny island on Michelin’s map. Two generations of a legendary culinary family pursue recognition on their own terms. Two chefs voluntarily give up their Star when they open a new restaurant and have just 52 days to win it back."

"One sandwich shop transforms into a fine-dining restaurant each night, while a young couple seeks to put Filipino cuisine at the center of one of America’s most competitive dining scenes. Their circumstances could hardly be more different, yet each faces the same uncertainty: when Michelin makes its decision, will everything they have strived for be enough?"
Ramsay noted that "Knife Edge" pulls back the curtain on the countless hours of preparation and discipline that diners rarely see before a meal reaches the table.

"Finally, now we have a show on Apple that really unfolds that unscripted drama and follows the highs and lows, the emotions, the pressures that these restaurants are under — especially today," he said.
The celebrity chef told Fox News Digital that he hopes the show gives viewers a new appreciation for the commitment behind every Michelin-starred meal.
Ramsay said he hopes viewers will appreciate the chef's pursuit of perfection. (Apple TV)

"I'd love the audience to take away from ‘Knife Edge' season 2 the understanding of pursuit for perfection and the price they pay is extraordinary," Ramsay said. "And then to understand properly, the commitment to perfection. You go to games and live sports, and you see that energy and the excitement and the touchdowns and the medals and the ceremony. title: Sylvester Stallone showered in his clothes to survive before ‘Rocky’ fame
summary: Sylvester Stallone's memoir "The Steps" reveals how he survived on raw eggs and cottage cheese in a tiny New York City apartment before "Rocky" fame.
story: Sylvester Stallone joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir, The Steps, opening up about his difficult upbringing, the lessons it taught him as a father and the personal experiences that inspired Rocky.

Before Sylvester Stallone became one of Hollywood's biggest stars, he had just $60 to his name — with $43.60 already set aside for rent. But even as he struggled to make ends meet in New York City, the future "Rocky" icon refused to give up on his dream.
In his new memoir, "The Steps," Stallone recounts the years before fame, including his arrival in New York City in 1969, determined to become an actor despite poverty, rejection and uncertainty.
The 80-year-old told Fox News Digital that even in his darkest moments, he held on to the belief that his life would eventually change for the better.
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The Steps: A Memoir" by Sylvester Stallone is out now. (William Morrow)

"I think it comes from naïveté and the folly of youth, that you still have this sense of, 'I can do it, I can break the mold,'" Stallone said. "I hadn't been beaten enough by life yet to say it's over because, as an actor, if you haven't made it by 30, I'd say 99% you're never going to make it. I wasn't aware of that, so I kept going."
Sylvester Stallone has written a new memoir, "The Steps: A Memoir." (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)

"In New York, when I was really down and out, I didn't focus on, 'God, you're going to be destitute,'" Stallone said. "There was this certain optimism that if you put every effort forward, if you denied yourself every moment of pleasure of going to the movies, dating a girl — if you abandoned all that and dedicate yourself, I believe that you'll know 100% whether you actually have a chance to be this character you always wished you could be."
Stallone never stopped believing he would one day make it as an actor.
WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

After leaving the American College in Switzerland without graduating and dropping out of the University of Miami just a few credits shy of a drama degree, Stallone returned to New York City with little to his name. He rented a room so cramped that he later compared it to the minimum size recommended for a federal jail cell. He shared a bathroom with 10 other people.

Stallone also found work as an usher at a movie theater, earning just $34 a week. He said the job became an education in filmmaking. Night after night, he studied the movies he watched, keeping his dream alive.
Sylvester Stallone is seen here in New York City. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Stallone said he would shower with his clothes on to save money on laundry. If he were lucky enough to find a bar of soap that didn't have a "strange hair" stuck to it, he would use it to lather up "my shirt, pants, underwear, socks — and myself."
Sylvester Stallone is seen here on Jan. 12, 1979. (Getty Images)

"I could never afford to go to a laundromat," Stallone said. "My wife thinks this is so gross, 'Why would you take a shower with your clothes on?' I said, 'It made sense to me at the time, rather than going down to the laundromat. But this was a tenement home. It was so bad. But you do what you could to survive.'"
To stave off hunger, Stallone would eat spoonfuls of cottage cheese, then down three or four raw eggs. In the book, he recalled later treating himself to chicken breast and apple juice.
Sylvester Stallone speaks onstage during "Sylvester Stallone In Conversation with Tracy Smith: The Steps" at 92NY on Sept. 28, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

"It's the only thing that made sense numerically, financially," he said. "Of course, it's all wrong. It's terrible. I'm surprised I didn't get salmonella, really. It's really quite remarkable. But these two things at a certain time of year, because in the summer, the cottage cheese would rot, and the eggs would spoil.

American actor Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith (1908-1997), watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the movie, "Rocky." (United Artists/Courtesy of Getty Images)

"But if you brought it from around October, it would sit on your windowsill until March. So that became my refrigerator. And at the time, I just thought it was so convenient. No dishes. You drink the egg, so you don't have to wash anything. You didn't need a fork. And the cottage cheese, it's a spoon, and you throw the cup away."
Sylvester Stallone is seen here in New York City. (Bettmann Archive)

Stallone wrote in the book, "I wouldn't recommend this diet to anyone. But if you're young and poor, it will suffice, which is why I used eating raw eggs in 'Rocky' to give some insight into Rocky's ways of approaching his life."
Stallone had a dollar or two a day for food. He needed a job, and fast.
American actor and screenwriter Sylvester Stallone on the set of "F.I.S.T.," directed by Norman Jewison. (Corbis via Getty Images)
One of Stallone's earliest gigs was cleaning the lion cages at Central Park Zoo. The smell was bad enough — but it wasn't what frightened him.

"I also feared for my life," he wrote. "The lions were always close by, always watching. They looked through me. They were behind a set of bars, but that didn't stop the great sad creatures from wedging their huge snouts between the bars to sniff me out. The way they inhaled and exhaled made an eerie moaning sound, like they already knew what I was going to taste like."
Sylvester Stallone was so broke when he married his first wife, Sasha Czack, in 1974, that he wore a movie costume. (Bettmann Archive)

During that period, Stallone faced repeated rejection from agents, including one who criticized his deep voice and asymmetrical mouth — two traits that would later become signatures of his screen persona.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Sylvester Stallone takes still photos on location while shooting a film in Dubuque. (Bettmann Archive)

Walking home one day, he spotted a "Help Wanted" sign at Dover Delicatessen and took the 6 p.m.-to-2 a.m. shift. While he was able to save enough money for a coat to brave the city's bitter winter, it's one gig he doesn't miss.

"Every customer gets cranky over this and that, 'Hey, there's not enough coleslaw here. This sandwich should weigh an ounce and a half more,'" Stallone said with a laugh. "You'd be shocked. I learned to be a really good fish cutter, like for lox on bagels. I still would hear, 'I can't see through the salmon.' They wanted the cut so thin that you could actually see light. Oh man. And you're cutting your fingers off, too."
After years of traveling in Europe, Sylvester Stallone returned to his birthplace, New York City, in 1969. (Bettmann Archive)

"And then the characters that come in at two in the morning, the outrageous drunks and gangsters, unbelievable," Stallone continued. "You'd be shocked who walks into a place at two in the morning and wants a sandwich. So that's colorful. And of course, I ended up in jail, but that's only because of the stupid deli."
American actor Sylvester Stallone sits on a staircase holding the leash of a dog wearing a football jersey in a still from the movie "Rocky." (Getty Images)
"I thought I was living OK, a decent life," he said. "But by today's standards, you were on the cusp of oblivion."

After an altercation at the deli, Stallone found himself handcuffed in the back of a police car, still wearing his apron and name tag. He was sent to "The Tombs," New York's notoriously violent detention facility — or, as Stallone put it, "the place of nightmares." He was put into a 20-foot-by-20-foot holding cell with at least 25 other men. One man was already pounding another's head into a small hole that prisoners used as a toilet.
Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" and starred as boxer Rocky Balboa. (Getty Images)
A criminal court judge eventually released Stallone.

American actor Sylvester Stallone appears with actor, director and screenwriter Woody Allen on the set of "Bananas." (Corbis via Getty Images)
"I took the apron, balled it up and tossed it in the trash on the way out the door," he wrote.
Today, Stallone has zero regrets.

"If you don't sacrifice completely and fail, you'll suffer for the rest of your life going, 'Why didn't I try harder? Why didn't I use whatever God-given talent I had to be the absolute best?'" Stallone said. "If you fail, you can say, 'I tried.' People can never point a finger in your face and say, 'You didn't try hard enough.' But my biggest fear was that I would leave something on the table."

Sylvester Stallone appears in a scene from "The Lords of Flatbush" (1974) after his girlfriend tells him she is pregnant, and he takes her to a jeweler to buy a ring. (FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)
Looking back, Stallone said those difficult years taught him a lesson that still resonates in "Rocky" decades later.

"'Rocky' still points out that if you're willing to completely sacrifice good times, pleasure and escapism for the goal, it's really possible," he said. "There is no halfway point."

title: ‘Double Lives of Suburban Wives’ star's staggering $550K month after leaving teaching for adult content
summary: Brianna Coppage reveals her best month earned $550,000 in adult content, dwarfing her former teacher salary after losing her school position.
story: Former high school English teacher Brianna Coppage tells Fox News Digital she earns more in one month than she made in a year teaching and explains why she would "never" return to the classroom.
Brianna Coppage may have lost her teaching career, but she certainly didn't take a pay cut.

The "Double Lives of Suburban Wives" star told Fox News Digital that her adult-content business has transformed her family's finances, revealing that her most successful month brought in a staggering $550,000.
"Oh, my best month was 550,000," Brianna told Fox News Digital.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR REVEALS STAGGERING $550K MONTH AFTER LEAVING TEACHING CAREER

The figure marks a dramatic departure from her former life as an English teacher at St. Clair High School in Franklin County, Missouri. In 2023, Coppage was placed on administrative leave after her adult-content work was discovered. She later resigned from her position.
Asked whether she now makes more in a single month than she previously earned in an entire year as a teacher, Brianna didn't hesitate.
"Yes," she said.
'DOUBLE LIVES' STAR SAYS BEING KICKED OUT OF CHURCH OVER ADULT CONTENT CAREER DIDN'T SHAKE HER FAITH
And despite the controversy that followed the end of her teaching career, Brianna said she wouldn't go back even if given the opportunity.
"Never. Never," she told Fox News Digital when asked whether she would accept her teaching job back tomorrow.
"Yeah, just the lifestyle and the time and being able to just be in control of myself and in my business," she continued. "It's changed my family's life and just everything for the better."

Brianna is one of the women featured on TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," which follows six couples in the St. Louis area navigating marriage, parenthood and suburban life while maintaining careers creating adult content.

According to TLC, what began as a financial pivot for Brianna and her husband, Phillip, quickly became a lucrative business. But that success came with consequences when Brianna's online career was publicly exposed and she lost her teaching job.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Brianna told Fox News Digital that she still struggles with whether losing her career was justified.

"I think… it's a difficult concept to even wrap my mind around," she said. "So obviously like professions have a level of professionalism, but also they couldn't cite anything that I technically broke."
"So was I really doing anything wrong? I don't know," she continued. "I think it's on a basis of morality."
Brianna also pushed back on what she described as a misconception surrounding her former employment.
"There was no like morality clause, which is a lot of… there's a misconception about that, that I signed something or a clause, a morality clause," she said. "There wasn't one. So I don't know."
While losing her teaching career forced Brianna onto a different professional path, she said the financial impact of her new work has been life-changing.
Brianna Coppage said working alongside husband Phillip has brought financial success while also testing boundaries within their marriage. (TLC)
"My family was able to pay off all of our debts. I paid off my student loans," she told Fox News Digital. "So I stopped putting groceries on credit cards."
"Like yeah, it just is so freeing, and I don't know, it's been life-changing."

That financial freedom is one of the central tensions explored on "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," where the women weigh the benefits of their unconventional careers against the judgment and loss of privacy that can accompany them.
For Brianna, the cost has been significant.

"I think the greatest thing it has cost me is the privacy, the lack of privacy," she told Fox News Digital.
Being thrust into the public eye has sometimes left her feeling as though people forget there's a person behind the headlines.
"And being in the public eye, it's like, I'm not a human anymore," Brianna said. "I'm not normal just like everybody else when truly I am. Like we are human beings too."
But when weighing that loss against what her new career has made possible for her family, Brianna said the benefits extend far beyond her income.
"I think the greatest thing it has afforded is just memories and time with my family that I wouldn't trade for the world," she said.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR OPENS UP ABOUT MARRIAGE ‘BETRAYAL’ AFTER ADULT-CONTENT CAREER CHANGES HER LIFE
Brianna said her own upbringing has shaped how she views the opportunities she can now provide for her children.
"Like growing up, I grew up fairly poor. And I mean family vacations and letting my kids experience things that I never would have is really priceless."
But despite the financial success and freedom Brianna says the career has given her family, she stopped short of saying she would encourage her daughter to follow the same path.

Asked how she would respond if her daughter came to her as an adult and said she wanted to pursue the same kind of work, Brianna said her first priority would be making sure she understood what she was getting into.
DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME
Promotional artwork for TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives." (TLC)
"I want to raise, you know, my daughter to be open-minded. Don't judge other people. It's OK if people are different," Brianna told Fox News Digital.
"So if she came to me, first, I would want her to have all the correct information. Is she safe?… It's not something that I'm going to encourage," Brianna said.
Still, she said she would offer her daughter the same acceptance she wants from others.
"But also just as I want people to love me and respect me and not judge me, I would give her that same…  that same love and respect."
Her success hasn't eliminated the complications that come with mixing marriage and business.

Brianna and Phillip's relationship became another major storyline on "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," with viewers watching the couple confront trust and boundary issues while simultaneously juggling life as parents and business partners.

"I think that with everything we're juggling, being parents, spouses, business partners, lifestyle, content creators, there is a lot to communicate about and a lot of boundaries to establish, and no relationship is perfect," she said.
She added that she was glad viewers were seeing some of those difficulties rather than an artificially polished version of their marriage.

"I like that this is on the show honestly, because it does show that no marriage is perfect and people go through struggles," Brianna said. "But I think at the end of the day, it matters how you work through that."
